1. Global Fuel Price Overview

Over 327 weekly observations spanning 84 countries, global retail fuel prices averaged $2.282/L for petrol, $2.134/L for diesel, and $1.711/L for LPG. Brent Crude, the global benchmark, averaged $106.69 per barrel across the period, oscillating between a COVID-19 trough of $47.97 (April 2020) and a 2022 crisis peak of $130.00 (March 2022).

The dataset captures extreme heterogeneity: petrol prices range from $0.010/L (Venezuela, heavily subsidized) to $6.779/L, while diesel spans $0.010/L to $6.240/L. This 600×+ range underscores how fiscal policy — not just crude markets — shapes what consumers pay at the pump.

2. Temporal Price Trends & Volatility

The weekly global average tracks Brent Crude with near-perfect correlation: r = 1.000 for petrol, diesel, and LPG. This relationship is not merely statistical — it is visible in the synchronized troughs and peaks across the six-year window.

COVID-19 Demand Shock (2020)

Between January and April 2020, Brent Crude fell 21.8% (from $66.65 to $52.12 per barrel). Global retail petrol followed almost one-for-one, dropping 21.7% (from $1.424 to $1.115/L). The April 2020 trough represents the lowest combined crude and retail price point in the entire dataset.

2022 Energy Crisis

Brent surged to $130.00/barrel in late March 2022, driven by supply disruptions. During March–May 2022, global average petrol reached $2.762/L — the highest sustained three-month average on record. Weekly volatility (standard deviation of week-over-week % change) averaged 1.55% for petrol, indicating sharp but relatively short-lived swings.

Post-Crisis Adjustment (2023–2026)

As Brent moderated from $117.12 (2022 average) to $104.43 (2023 average), retail petrol eased 10.8% — again tracking crude almost exactly. By 2026, both crude and retail prices had settled at new elevated plateaus above pre-pandemic levels.

3. Regional Price Disparities

Europe and Oceania consistently record the highest retail fuel prices, while the Middle East and South America sit at the opposite extreme. Over the full period, Europe averaged $3.70/L for petrol versus $1.23/L in the Middle East — a 3.0× differential.

The regional price spread (difference between the highest and lowest regional annual average) widened from $1.61/L in 2020 to $2.87/L in 2026. This divergence is driven primarily by differing tax and subsidy regimes, not crude access costs, since Brent is a global benchmark.

4. Impact of Subsidies and Taxation on Retail Prices

Subsidy regimes are the single most powerful determinant of retail price levels after the crude benchmark itself. Countries classified as High subsidy (including "Very High") averaged $0.454/L for petrol, while Low subsidy countries averaged $2.931/L — a dampening effect of 84.5%. The effect is nearly identical across diesel (84.9%) and LPG (84.5%).

Price Pass-Through: Do Subsidies Buffer Volatility?

Yes, but imperfectly. The Brent-to-retail correlation in High-subsidy countries is 0.253 versus 0.416 in Low-subsidy countries. Subsidies therefore cut pass-through by roughly 40% in correlation terms. However, even subsidized markets are not fully insulated: when Brent moves sharply, some leakage into retail prices still occurs.

Figure 7. Average retail prices by subsidy regime. High-subsidy countries show ~85% lower prices across all fuel types.
Figure 8. Brent-to-petrol correlation by income level and subsidy regime. Low-subsidy countries exhibit substantially higher pass-through regardless of income.

The Tax Dimension

Taxation operates as the mirror image of subsidies: it raises prices above crude-refining costs. High-income countries levy an average tax of 34.7% on retail fuel, compared to 22.9% in low-income countries and 21.1% in middle-income countries. Oceania (38.7%) and Europe (34.6%) lead globally in tax incidence, while South America (18.2%) and the Middle East (19.6%) impose the lightest tax burdens — consistent with their lower average retail prices.

5. Fuel Affordability by Income Level

Retail fuel prices are strongly stratified by national income. High-income countries average $3.55/L for petrol — 2.6× the $1.39/L observed in low-income countries and 2.2× the $1.59/L in middle-income countries. This pattern holds across all three fuel types and reflects the combined effect of higher taxation and lower subsidy penetration in wealthier economies.

Energy equity implications are stark: while high-income consumers face higher absolute prices, they also benefit from more stable pricing (lower coefficient of variation in non-subsidized markets) and greater fiscal capacity to absorb shocks. Low-income consumers in low-subsidy regimes face both higher relative burdens and greater volatility.

6. Key Findings & Policy Implications

Crude-to-retail pass-through is near-perfect at the global level. Weekly Brent Crude and global average retail prices move in lockstep (r ≈ 1.000). Policymakers should treat crude price forecasts as direct inputs to consumer cost projections, not merely as market background.
Subsidies are the most effective price-dampening tool available. High-subsidy countries realize an 84.5% reduction in average petrol prices relative to low-subsidy peers, and cut Brent pass-through correlation by ~40%. For consumer protection, targeted subsidy mechanisms outperform broad tax cuts in shielding vulnerable households.
Tax policy is the primary driver of cross-country dispersion above crude costs. High-income countries tax fuel at 34.7% on average versus ~22% in low- and middle-income countries. Tax calibration offers a direct lever for revenue generation, demand management, and environmental objectives — but must be balanced against affordability concerns.
Regional price inequality is widening. The spread between the most and least expensive regions grew from $1.61/L (2020) to $2.87/L (2026). Divergent fiscal paths — Europe raising taxes, the Middle East maintaining subsidies — are entrenching a two-tier global fuel market.
Low-subsidy, low-income countries face a double burden. They exhibit higher price volatility (higher coefficient of variation) and weaker fiscal capacity to deploy counter-cyclical support. International financing mechanisms for energy price stabilization should prioritize this cohort.
Subsidy design matters more than subsidy level. Even within high-subsidy regimes, pass-through correlations vary (0.23–0.30). Automatic pricing formulas, buffer funds, and transparent adjustment mechanisms can improve stabilization without raising fiscal costs.

Recommendations for Policymakers

  • Adopt automatic pricing formulas tied to rolling-average crude benchmarks rather than spot prices. This smooths volatility while retaining market alignment.
  • Target subsidies to vulnerable households via cash transfers or ration cards rather than universal price caps, which disproportionately benefit wealthier consumers with higher vehicle ownership.
  • Build fiscal buffers during low-crude periods (e.g., 2020–2021) to fund subsidy drawdowns or tax holidays during price spikes, reducing procyclical fiscal stress.
  • Harmonize tax and subsidy data reporting across ministries to enable real-time monitoring of pass-through rates — a critical early warning indicator for policy leakage.
  • Evaluate subsidy sustainability against medium-term crude price scenarios. With Brent settling above $120/barrel in 2026, high-subsidy regimes face escalating fiscal exposure if crude remains elevated.
Data source: Global Fuel Prices 2020–2026 (Kaggle / belbino). Analysis covers 84 countries, 27,468 weekly observations, and 7 geographic regions.
